newsitem.title: New Zealand: PRESS DIGEST - NZ Business weeklies - Mar 7.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - NZ Business weeklies - Mar 7.

text.p: Wine-box inquiry evidence took a dramatic turn on Thursday when Serious Fraud Office chief investigator Geoff Downey revealed director Chas Sturt had blocked an investigation into possible fraud at Bank of New Zealand. Downey, appearing on subpoena, revealed that he had first been informed of possible fraud within BNZ in mid-1992. A series of investigations began which, at that stage, had been authorised by Sturt. Page 1.

Aotearoa Television executive Eric McPhee signed a declaration of trust for former director Derek Burn's shareholding in an associate company but denies anything similar was done for New Zealand First MP Tukoroirangi Morgan. McPhee said he was approached by Burns who asked him to hold shares in trust in ATN holding company Pumanawa Holdings on his behalf, saying it was normal business practice. McPhee took legal advice before signing which confirmed this and has subsequently signed an affidavit giving details of the transaction. Page 1.

Treasurer Winston Peters' popularity continues to tumble since he became deputy prime minister and he is now by far the most unpopular political leader with two out of three adults giving him the thumbs down. The latest National Business Review-Consultus poll reveals his standing slumped a further six points since the coalition deal with National was signed in December and now just 27 percent have a somewhat favourable or very favourable view of him. Page 1.

At the same time that INL's $700 million bid for Sky Television was falling over last week, Rupert Murdoch was celebrating a deal worth only twice as much giving his satellite television channels access to 75 percent of homes in the U.S. Shares in Murdoch's News Corporation jumped sharply on the announcement of its purchase of 50 percent of EchoStar Communications for US$1 billion in cash and satellites. Page 3.

The Dairy Board may still have to answer to alleged breaches of U.S. antitrust laws, despite a U.S. district court's landmark ruling that the board is exempt from those laws. Counsel for the company alleging the breaches said an appeal of the judge's decision would be filed this week. The case began as a commercial dispute over a consignment of cheese. Early in 1993, Trugman-Nash and Trio Cheese Imports received about US$2 million worth of cheese. They later sold it but did not pay the Dairy Board's subsidairies, Western Dairy Products and Milk Products Holdings. Trugman-Nash claimed the board failed to deliver a contract for a quantity of cheese, which amounted to a breach of antitrust laws, fraud and breach of contract. Page 5.

Rising tensions as the wine-box inquiry nears its conclusion boiled over this week as European Pacific made a stinging attack on the commission of inquiry and its staff. With Serious Fraud Office director Chas Sturt still missing in action with a doctor's certificate, the commission slotted in time to hear European Pacific and Fay Richwhite open and close their cases. For European Pacific, Richard Craddock QC wasted no time tearing strips off the commission. Page 11.

The government has again warned the major telecommunications companies to make progress on interconnection disputes. Addressing the Telecommunications Users' Association annual meeting in Wellington this week, Communications Minister Maurice Williamson said the major players in the market were acting like "teenagers". "They know their own rights backwards but give scant thought to anyone else's rights in the process, particularly users' interests," he said. Page 11.

Turners & Growers has sold 2.4 hectares overlooking Auckland's Viaduct Basin to Pacific Development & Investment Corporation for $17.1 million after a $22 million deal negotiated last year fell through. The property, former home to Auckland's old city markets, is a prime site close to the proposed America's Cup village. Page 12.

Brierley Investments-owned Union Shipping and Austalia New Zealand Direct Line began their merged Tasman operation this week under a new name, Union Direct Line. New Zealand general manager Michelle England said the UDL branding would be used solely in marketing transtasman services and ANZDL would remain the line's name in the North America and Pacific trades. Page 14.
